strong a-/ō-stem adjective.mapping_rationale: Wright treats the strong declension as partly nominal and partly pronominal, and says it is divided into pure a-/ō-stems, ja-/jō-stems, and wa-/wō-stems. §§424-431 cover the main pure a-/ō-stem adjective patterns, including short stems, long stems, h-stems such as hēah, and disyllabic types such as halig.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
strong ja-/jō-stem adjective.mapping_rationale: Wright explicitly treats ja-/jō-stem adjectives in §§432-434. The class differs from long pure a-/ō-stems chiefly in the masculine nominative singular, neuter nominative/accusative singular and plural, and feminine nominative singular.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
strong wa-/wō-stem adjective.mapping_rationale: Wright treats wa-/wō-stem adjectives in §§435-437. Gearu is the main paradigm type; §436 lists similar short wa-stem adjectives such as geolu, fealu, nearu, and salu.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
strong i-stem adjective.mapping_rationale: Wright says original adjective i-stems mostly passed into the ja-declension in prehistoric Old English, but §438 preserves the historical category and examples such as blīþe, clǣne, grēne, scīene, and swēte.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
strong u-stem adjective.mapping_rationale: Wright says only traces of the old adjective u-declension survive, especially cwicu/cucu 'alive' and wlacu 'warm'; most other old u-stem adjectives passed into the a-, ja-, or wa-declension.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt

weak adjective.mapping_rationale: Wright §440 gives the weak adjective paradigm and notes that weak adjectives largely use the same endings as weak nouns, except that adjectives generally use genitive plural -ra rather than -(e)na. Modern teaching grammars use the weak label for adjectives after demonstratives, possessives, and other definite contexts.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
present participle adjective.mapping_rationale: Wright §441 treats present participles as adjectival in declension: the present participle can be declined strong or weak like an ordinary adjective, though predicative uses may remain uninflected.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
past participle adjective.mapping_rationale: Wright §442 treats past participles as declined strong or weak like ordinary adjectives; strong past participles follow manig or halig depending on stem quantity.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt

regular comparative.mapping_rationale: Wright §443 treats the comparative degree. Comparatives are historically weak in the oldest Germanic periods; Old English Online likewise states that comparative adjectives always decline weak.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
umlauted comparative.mapping_rationale: Wright §443 lists common comparatives with umlaut, including eald → ieldra, geong → gingra/giengra, lang → lengra, sceort → sciertra, and strang → strengra.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
Old English Online. (n.d.). Comparatives and superlatives. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://oldenglish.info/adj4.html
regular superlative.mapping_rationale: Wright §444 treats the superlative degree. Unlike comparatives, superlatives can be declined strong or weak depending on syntax; Old English Online explicitly notes this contrast.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
umlauted superlative.mapping_rationale: This is the superlative counterpart to the umlauted comparative type. Wright §444 covers superlative formation; for implementation it is useful to track adjectives whose comparative/superlative stems show i-mutation.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
suppletive or irregular comparison.mapping_rationale: Wright §445 lists irregular comparison patterns such as gōd with betera/bettra and betst, lȳtel with lǣssa/lǣst, micel with māra/mǣst, and yfel with wiersa/wierrest.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
adverbial or prepositional comparison.mapping_rationale: Wright §446 treats comparatives and superlatives formed from adverbs or prepositions, often with superlatives in -mest/-emest, such as æfterra/æftemest and innemest.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
cardinal numeral adjective.mapping_rationale: Wright includes numerals inside the adjective chapter. §§447-452 cover cardinal and ordinal numerals.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
ordinal numeral adjective.mapping_rationale: Ordinals are adjectival in function and are treated by Wright in the numeral section of the adjective chapter.

references: Wright, J., & Wright, E. M. (1914). Old English grammar (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. Retrieved July 3, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/oldenglishgramma00wrig/oldenglishgramma00wrig_djvu.txt
other numeral adjective.mapping_rationale: Wright §§453-457 treat other numeral formations after cardinals and ordinals.
